A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same KomplexNet study. Their main texts, equations, figures, table, and appendices are readable and can be matched despite additions and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original classification and phase-synchrony experiments, including robustness, digit-count generalization, CIFAR backgrounds, and moving digits.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds results for capacity-matched baselines and a fixed Gaussian coupling-kernel variant.

M1.justification: Appendix A.5 adds a tested variant whose Gaussian coupling kernel remains fixed during training. The main learned-kernel architectures, feedback updates, losses, and Algorithms 1–2 remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Multi-MNIST, overlapping and noisy digits, two-to-nine-digit evaluation, CIFAR backgrounds, and moving digits already appear in v1. The new controls and stimulus illustrations introduce no additional task or dataset coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds a larger real-valued model explicitly matched to KomplexNet's parameter count and a comparably sized Vision Transformer. Figure 12 evaluates both on in-distribution, overlapping-digit, and noisy-image tests, substantially broadening the original real/random-phase/ideal-phase comparisons.

E3.justification: The added comparisons introduce capacity matching and a 50-epoch ViT training budget; the new ablation holds coupling weights fixed. Existing data-generation procedures and metrics are retained. The newly disclosed 30 epochs for other models do not establish a change to their earlier training.

E4.justification: Appendix A.5 and Figures 16–17 add a targeted ablation testing what synchronization and accuracy remain without learning the coupling kernel, including layerwise phase visualizations. Existing feedback-layer, extended-timestep, robustness, and moving-digit analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report means and standard deviations over 50 random initializations and supplementary results for the best validation model. The additional results follow this existing practice; no new uncertainty-estimation or significance-testing procedure is introduced.

E6.justification: Figure 12 adds results showing the new real-valued and ViT baselines below KomplexNets on overlap and noise. Figures 16–17 show that fixed coupling supports improvement over time but yields weaker synchrony and lower final accuracy than learned coupling. These substantially extend the evidence; retained KomplexNet curves do not demonstrate a version-to-version performance gain.

T1.justification: Section 6.2 adds graph-based Kuramoto dynamics, an energy function, and an asserted gradient-flow interpretation in Equations 8–9. This is new mathematical reasoning, although no proof or conditions reconciling it with the model's asymmetric coupling are supplied. Equations 1–7 remain unchanged.

C1.justification: The abstract, four introduction contributions, and Section 6.1 retain the central claims about synchrony-assisted classification, robustness, generalization, and feedback benefits. The additional controls support these existing contributions; replacing 'real-valued counterparts' with 'baseline' principally clarifies comparator wording.

C2.justification: v2 substantially expands interpretations of ambiguous-boundary phase blending, feedback through predictive coding, disentanglement, and graph clustering. Section 6.2 also adds scaling arguments and speculative symbolic and multimodal extensions, while Appendix A.5 interprets the respective contributions of synchronization dynamics and learned coupling.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-availability link and discloses training durations of 50 epochs for ViT versus 30 for other models. Conversely, Table 1 replaces four feedback-model epsilon values, previously 0.4 or 0.5, with unexplained dashes, reducing hyperparameter documentation without establishing an actual procedural change.

R1.justification: Sections 3 and 6.2 broaden positioning from Gestalt-oriented binding toward traveling waves, modern oscillatory neuroscience, predictive coding, and symbolic binding. Numerous substantive citations are added, including Jacobs et al. (2025), Rao and Ballard (1999), Löwe et al. (2024), and Smolensky (1990).

P1.justification: Section 3 is retitled and substantially rewritten, and Section 6.2 develops a much broader multi-topic narrative. The gating explanation, ambiguous-phase discussion, and moving-digit appendix are also revised, materially changing the exposition despite preserving the overall section sequence.

P2.justification: v2 adds multi-panel comparison and ablation displays in Figures 12, 16, and 17, plus stimulus examples in Figures 18–19. Several retained plots receive clearer loss-axis labels and revised placement or captions. Figure 19's changed comparator description is inconsistent with its unchanged plot.

improvement.justification: The additional capacity-matched comparisons, fixed-kernel ablation, and code pointer strengthen empirical support and accessibility. However, the new gradient-flow argument omits conditions needed to reconcile it with Figure 9's asymmetric couplings, Table 1 loses feedback hyperparameters, and Figure 19 incorrectly describes the retained dynamic-versus-static comparison as comparison with the real-valued baseline. These mathematical and reporting regressions counter the empirical gains, leaving the net quality direction uncertain.
